title: finding(types/components): `PageNodeSchema.body` is array-only while its only reader casts around that to accept a single node — and the root README's flagship example authors the refused form
body:
Found while covering the root `README.md` for #5174 (batch 37, the last ledger row). Filed unassigned and NOT repaired there: that card is scoped to making the page's snippets compile, and this is a shipped TYPE surface whose repair is a decision about which side is right.

## What

`PageNodeSchema` narrows the content channel it inherits, and the only reader of that channel contradicts the narrowing.

```
packages/types/src/base.ts    BaseSchema.body?:      SchemaNode | SchemaNode[]
packages/types/src/layout.ts  PageNodeSchema.body?:  SchemaNode[]            (narrowed to array-only)
```

The reader — `FlatContent`, the legacy body/children path in `packages/components/src/renderers/layout/page.tsx` — explicitly supports the single-node form, and needs a cast to say so, because its own declared input forbids it:

```
const content = schema.body || schema.children;
const nodes: SchemaNode[] = Array.isArray(content)
  ? content
  : content
    ? [content as SchemaNode]     (the cast exists only because the declaration says array)
    : [];
```

`PageRenderer`'s props are `schema: PageNodeSchema`, so the branch that handles a single node is unreachable through its own declared type. It is reachable in practice, because nothing on the authoring path is annotated `PageNodeSchema`.

## Measured (on `0ea7054f8`, through the doc-snippet gate's own program)

The root README's flagship "Basic Usage" example authors exactly the refused shape — `body` as one object, not an array:

```
const schema = { type: "page", title: "Dashboard", body: { type: "grid", ... } }
```

It type-checks today only because `SchemaRendererProps.schema` is declared `BaseSchema | string | null | undefined` — the WIDER parent — and `BaseSchema` carries `[key: string]: any`. Length-preserving decimal probes on that literal, run through `compileSnippets` at `0ea7054f8`:

- outer `type` key renamed: RED, `TS2322 ... Property 'type' is missing ... but required in type 'BaseSchema'`
- outer `type` value made a number: RED, `TS2322 ... Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'`
- sibling `columns` key renamed: GREEN — the index signature absorbs it
- nested `items[].label` renamed: GREEN

So `type` is the ONE member checked, and `body`'s arity is checked by nothing on the authoring path. Annotating that same literal `PageNodeSchema` — the type of the node it is — turns the landing page's own example RED. That is why batch 37 left the literal at `BaseSchema` and filed this instead of "repairing" the example into the array form: the example matches the runtime, and the declaration does not.

## Why it matters

An author who DOES reach for the precise type (the shape a contract-first host wants, and the shape the renderer's own props use) is refused for a value the renderer handles. An author who does not gets no check at all. Both halves point at the same open question, and neither is answerable from the doc side.

## The decision, not made here

1. Widen `PageNodeSchema.body` back to `SchemaNode | SchemaNode[]`, matching `BaseSchema` and the runtime, and drop `FlatContent`'s cast. Cheapest; keeps the landing page's example legal; keeps two arities alive on one key.
2. Keep `body` array-only and make the runtime agree — `FlatContent` stops accepting a bare node, the root README and every other single-node example move to the array form. Contract-first, and it invalidates authored metadata that works today.

Adjacent, not the same card: #8284 (`BaseSchema` declares `body` and `children` without saying which renderer reads which) is about WHICH channel; this one is about the ARITY of one of them.
